title: Why Kids with Autism Are Getting Special Swim Lessons in Florida
summary: Did you know that water can feel amazing to some kids? For many children with autism, the sparkle and pressure of water is soothing. But there's a scary fact: kids with autism are 160 times more likely to drown than other kids. In Florida, where there are pools and beaches everywhere, this is a big worry. Five-year-old Mackenzie Wesley loves the water. She wears a big grin and Lilo & Stitch swim gear to her lessons. Her mom, Brittany Bucknor, knows the danger. "In Florida, there's water everywhere," she says. "Kids on the spectrum have a way higher rate of drowning." That's because about half of autistic children might wander away from safe places. If they find water, it can be dangerous. But quality swim lessons can help. Florida has a new law that gives parents information about drowning prevention and a voucher for swim lessons. The voucher is about $200 for up to eight lessons. Mackenzie goes to the YMCA of South Florida, which has a special program called Swim Buddies. The program gives one-on-one lessons tailored to each child. Instructors use toys and games to make kids feel safe. They teach skills like waiting to be told it's okay to enter the water. Tania Santiago Perez, a professor who studies these lessons, says kids can improve in just five or six sessions. The program is overwhelmed with requests, but it's saving lives.
why_it_matters: Knowing how to be safe around water is important for everyone — and if a friend at your pool needs extra help, these programs make sure they can learn too.

background_read: Florida (a state in the southeastern U.S. surrounded by ocean and full of pools) has one of the highest numbers of drowning deaths for young children.
Kids with autism often enjoy water because the sparkle and pressure feel soothing, but they may also wander away from safe places — making pools extra dangerous.
Organizations like the YMCA (a community group that runs gyms and swim programs) now create special one‑on‑one lessons that turn safety into games.
Article_Structure: WHO: A five‑year‑old girl with autism, Mackenzie, her mom, and swim instructors at the YMCA of South Florida.
WHAT: Florida is using a new law that gives out vouchers for swim lessons designed just for autistic children, to lower the high drowning risk.
WHERE: In Florida, where pools and beaches are everywhere, especially at the YMCA of South Florida’s Swim Buddies program.
WHY: Because about half of autistic kids might wander toward water, and tailored lessons teach them skills like waiting for permission so they stay safe.

perspectives.description: Parents and kids feel more confident because the one‑on‑one lessons are fun and teach life‑saving habits. Mackenzie’s mom now has real hope.
The Swim Buddies program is overwhelmed with requests, so many families who want the lessons can’t get in right away. The $200 voucher also may not cover all the lessons some children need.

Researchers believe that with the right approach, all kids can learn water safety. This makes it a question of whether enough programs and money will be set aside so every at‑risk child gets a chance.
